<!-- data-checksum: c54ef1144cca5064aaabf104b2604dc4 -->

The same patients measured **three or more times** (before surgery, then at 6 weeks, 3 months and 1 year), or **matched sets** of three or more patients. This is [page 7](07-two-paired-groups.qmd) extended past two measurements. As on [page 8](08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd), each test asks one question first: **does the outcome differ anywhere among the visits (or groups)?** [Which visits differ?](#which-groups-differ) explains what to do next.

::: {.callout-note}
## 💡 How every section on this page works
Each section answers one question about one of the practice's datasets: the joint replacement PROMs and matched sets, or the boot vs cast trial from [page 6](06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#unpaired-t). Its first code block loads the packages and the data, so you can jump straight to the section you need. Run that section's blocks in order, top to bottom.

To keep the code short, the joint replacement examples use every case, including the 80 patients who had both sides operated on. In a real study, decide how to handle them ([page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd#paired)) and say what you did.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: these tests drop anyone with a missed visit
Repeated-measures ANOVA, the Friedman test and Cochran's Q need every patient measured at **every** visit. A patient who missed one visit is dropped completely, along with their other measurements. Below, 574 patients had a pre-op PROMIS physical function score, but only 328 had all four, so the analysis loses 246 patients (43%). If the patients who miss visits differ from those who don't, the result is biased. [Mixed models](../beyond/16-mixed-models.qmd#why-mixed-models) use everyone's available data, and are usually the better choice for repeated PROMs.
:::

## Repeated-measures ANOVA {#repeated-measures-anova}

**The question:** Does physical function (PROMIS-29+2) change over the first year after surgery?

### When to use it

- A **measurement** taken **three or more times** on the same patients (or once on each member of a matched set).
- The changes between visits are roughly normal, or there are plenty of patients.
- **Sphericity:** the spread of the changes is similar for every pair of visits. Mauchly's test checks it; if it fails, the **Greenhouse-Geisser** correction adjusts the degrees of freedom. Both programs below report both.
- Only patients measured at **every** visit are included (see the warning above).
- If the outcome is skewed, bounded or ordinal → the [Friedman test](#friedman).

PROMIS physical function is a T-score: 50 is the average of the US general population. The four-question form in PROMIS-29+2 runs from 22.5 to 57.0, and 57.0 is the best it can record.

### Look at the data first

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

pf <- proms |>
  select(case_id, visit, promis_pf) |>
  group_by(case_id) |>
  filter(all(!is.na(promis_pf))) |>     # keep patients measured at all four visits
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr")))   # in time order

n_distinct(pf$case_id)                # patients with complete data
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 328
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(pf, aes(visit, promis_pf)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Visit", y = "PROMIS physical function (T-score)")
```

## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd
import pingouin as pg
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")
visits = ["preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"]   # in time order

pf = proms[["case_id", "visit", "promis_pf"]]
complete = pf.groupby("case_id")["promis_pf"].transform(lambda scores: scores.notna().all())
pf = pf[complete]                        # keep patients measured at all four visits

print(pf["case_id"].nunique())            # patients with complete data
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
328
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
parts = ax.boxplot([pf.loc[pf["visit"] == v, "promis_pf"] for v in visits], tick_labels=visits)   # naming the result keeps it out of the output
ax.set_xlabel("Visit")
ax.set_ylabel("PROMIS physical function (T-score)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](09-three-plus-matched_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png)
:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(pf.groupby("visit")["promis_pf"].agg(["mean", "std"]).loc[visits])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
            mean       std
visit                     
preop  36.129573  5.439515
6wk    39.413110  5.530713
3mo    44.862805  5.549253
1yr    48.152744  5.594432
```


:::

:::

328 patients were measured at all four visits. Their mean T-score climbs at every visit, and the spreads stay similar. At 1 year, 28 of them sit at 57.0, the best the form can record.

### Run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pf_anova <- rstatix::anova_test(data = pf, dv = promis_pf, wid = case_id, within = visit,
                                 effect.size = c("pes", "ges"))   # partial and generalized eta squared
pf_anova
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
ANOVA Table (type III tests)

$ANOVA
  Effect DFn DFd       F         p p<.05   pes   ges
1  visit   3 981 326.125 7.55e-147     * 0.499 0.417

$`Mauchly's Test for Sphericity`
  Effect     W     p p<.05
1  visit 0.995 0.903      

$`Sphericity Corrections`
  Effect   GGe       DF[GG]     p[GG] p[GG]<.05   HFe      DF[HF]     p[HF]
1  visit 0.997 2.99, 977.78 2.23e-146         * 1.007 3.02, 987.8 7.55e-147
  p[HF]<.05
1         *
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
pf_anova = pg.rm_anova(data=pf, dv="promis_pf", within="visit", subject="case_id",
                        correction=True, effsize="np2", detailed=True)   # np2 = partial eta squared
print(pf_anova.T)    # .T turns the wide table on its side, so it fits
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                       0             1
Source             visit         Error
SS          28577.956425  28654.621075
DF                     3           981
MS           9525.985475     29.209604
F             326.125121           NaN
p_unc                0.0           NaN
p_GG_corr            0.0           NaN
np2              0.49933           NaN
eps             0.996718           NaN
sphericity          True           NaN
W_spher          0.99515           NaN
p_spher         0.903231           NaN
```


:::
:::

:::





### Read the output

- **F = 326.1, with 3 and 981 degrees of freedom** (DFn/DFd in R, DF in Python): how much the visit means differ, compared with how much each patient's scores bounce around their own average. 3 = four visits minus one; 981 = 3 × (328 patients − 1).
- **p** (R prints `7.55e-147`; pingouin's table rounds it to `0.0` in the `p_unc` row): far below 0.001.
- **Mauchly's test, W = 0.995, p = 0.903:** no evidence that sphericity is violated, so the uncorrected result stands.
- **Sphericity corrections** (R) or **eps** and **p_GG_corr** (Python): the Greenhouse-Geisser epsilon is 0.997 (1 means perfect sphericity), and the corrected p-value is still far below 0.001.
- **pes = 0.499** (R) or **np2** (Python): partial eta squared, below.

### Effect size and 95% CI

**Partial eta squared (η²~p~)** is the share of the within-patient variation that the visits account for. As a rough guide, 0.01 is small, 0.06 medium and 0.14 large. **Generalized eta squared** (ges = 0.417 in R) also counts the differences *between* patients, which makes it comparable with designs that aren't repeated measures; report it when readers will compare studies of different designs.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pf_model <- aov(promis_pf ~ visit + Error(case_id / visit), data = pf)   # the same ANOVA in base R
effectsize::eta_squared(pf_model, partial = TRUE)                         # with a 95% CI
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# Effect Size for ANOVA (Type I)

Group         | Parameter | Eta2 (partial) |       95% CI
---------------------------------------------------------
case_id:visit |     visit |           0.50 | [0.47, 1.00]

- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
print(pf_anova.loc[0, "np2"])    # pingouin doesn't compute a CI for it
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
0.4993302359186056
```


:::
:::

:::

η²~p~ = 0.49: a very large effect. The visits account for about half of the variation in each patient's scores over the year.

### How to report it

> **Methods:** PROMIS-29+2 physical function T-scores across the four visits were compared with one-way repeated-measures ANOVA in patients with all four measurements. Sphericity was assessed with Mauchly's test, with the Greenhouse-Geisser correction planned if it was violated. Partial eta squared (η²~p~) is reported as the effect size.
>
> **Results:** Of 574 patients with a pre-op PROMIS physical function score, 328 had all four measurements. Their mean T-score was 36.1 (SD 5.4) before surgery, 39.4 (SD 5.5) at 6 weeks, 44.9 (SD 5.5) at 3 months and 48.2 (SD 5.6) at 1 year (F(3, 981) = 326.1, p < 0.001; η²~p~ = 0.50, one-sided 95% CI 0.47 to 1.00; Mauchly's test of sphericity p = 0.903).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: a significant F doesn't say which visits differ
The ANOVA says physical function changed somewhere over the year. To say *when*, compare the visits with paired tests and a correction for multiple comparisons ([page 15](../beyond/15-post-hoc.qmd#after-repeated-measures-anova)). And remember who's missing: the 246 patients without complete data may have recovered differently.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: which tools check sphericity
- **R:** base `aov(... + Error(case_id / visit))` gives the same F test but ignores sphericity; `rstatix::anova_test()` adds Mauchly's test and the corrections. rstatix rounds its numbers to 3 decimals.
- **Python:** pingouin's `rm_anova(correction=True)` reports Mauchly's test and the Greenhouse-Geisser correction. statsmodels' `AnovaRM` gives the F test only.
- **Effect sizes:** pingouin returns either partial (`effsize="np2"`) or generalized (`effsize="ng2"`) eta squared; rstatix returns both if asked.
:::

## Friedman test {#friedman}

**The question:** With a removable boot, does the EFAS score keep changing between 6 weeks, 3 months and 12 months?

### When to use it

- An outcome measured **three or more times** on the same patients, when it's **skewed**, **ordinal** or has a **ceiling or floor**. The EFAS score adds up six questions, and by 12 months scores crowd toward its maximum of 24.
- It ranks each patient's own scores (1st, 2nd, 3rd) and asks whether some visits tend to rank higher than others.
- Only patients measured at **every** visit are included.
- If the outcome is a roughly normal measurement → [repeated-measures ANOVA](#repeated-measures-anova).

### Look at the data first

The boot arm of the trial from [page 6](06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#unpaired-t) has 60 randomized patients, and some missed visits.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

trial <- read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)   # one row per patient and visit

efas_boot <- trial |>
  filter(arm == "boot", visit %in% c("6wk", "3mo", "12mo")) |>
  select(patient_id, visit, efas) |>
  group_by(patient_id) |>
  filter(all(!is.na(efas))) |>           # keep patients measured at all three visits
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = c("6wk", "3mo", "12mo")))

n_distinct(efas_boot$patient_id)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 50
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(efas_boot, aes(visit, efas)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Visit", y = "EFAS score (24 = best)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](09-three-plus-matched_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
efas_boot |>
  group_by(visit) |>
  summarise(median = median(efas), q1 = quantile(efas, 0.25), q3 = quantile(efas, 0.75))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  visit median    q1    q3
  <fct>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 6wk     12.5    11    14
2 3mo     17      16    20
3 12mo    20      19    22
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd
import pingouin as pg
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

trial = pd.read_csv("data/foot_ankle_rct_long.csv")   # one row per patient and visit
visits = ["6wk", "3mo", "12mo"]

efas_boot = trial[(trial["arm"] == "boot") & trial["visit"].isin(visits)][["patient_id", "visit", "efas"]]
complete = efas_boot.groupby("patient_id")["efas"].transform(lambda scores: scores.notna().all())
efas_boot = efas_boot[complete]           # keep patients measured at all three visits

print(efas_boot["patient_id"].nunique())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
50
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
parts = ax.boxplot([efas_boot.loc[efas_boot["visit"] == v, "efas"] for v in visits], tick_labels=visits)
ax.set_xlabel("Visit")
ax.set_ylabel("EFAS score (24 = best)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](09-three-plus-matched_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png)
:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(efas_boot.groupby("visit")["efas"].describe()[["25%", "50%", "75%"]].loc[visits])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
        25%   50%   75%
visit                  
6wk    11.0  12.5  14.0
3mo    16.0  17.0  20.0
12mo   19.0  20.0  22.0
```


:::
:::

:::

50 of the 60 patients randomized to a boot were measured at all three visits. Scores rise at each visit, and by 12 months they're crowding the ceiling of 24: 6 patients score the maximum.

### Run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
efas_test <- friedman.test(efas ~ visit | patient_id, data = efas_boot)   # outcome ~ visit | patient
efas_test
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Friedman rank sum test

data:  efas and visit and patient_id
Friedman chi-squared = 84.942, df = 2, p-value < 2.2e-16
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
efas_test = pg.friedman(data=efas_boot, dv="efas", within="visit", subject="patient_id")
print(efas_test)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
         Source         W  ddof1          Q         p_unc
Friedman  visit  0.849424      2  84.942408  3.589140e-19
```


:::
:::

:::





### Read the output

- **Friedman chi-squared = 84.9** (R) or **Q** (Python): how consistently the visits rank in the same order across patients.
- **df = 2:** three visits minus one.
- **p < 0.001** (R prints "p < 2.2e-16").
- **W = 0.849** (Python): Kendall's W, below.

### Effect size and 95% CI

**Kendall's W** measures how consistently patients' scores rank the visits in the same order: 0 means no agreement at all, 1 means every patient's scores rank the three visits identically. As a rough guide, 0.1 is small, 0.3 moderate and 0.5 large.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# kendalls_w() warns when a patient has the same score at two visits; the tie correction already handles that
set.seed(2026)   # its CI comes from a bootstrap (random resampling); a seed makes it repeatable
effectsize::kendalls_w(efas ~ visit | patient_id, data = efas_boot)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Kendall's W |       95% CI
--------------------------
0.85        | [0.78, 1.00]

- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
print(efas_test["W"])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Friedman    0.849424
Name: W, dtype: float64
```


:::
:::

:::





W = 0.85: a large effect. Most patients improved from each visit to the next. R's CI comes from a bootstrap, which is why the code sets a seed; pingouin doesn't compute one.

### How to report it

> **Methods:** Because EFAS scores crowd toward the ceiling of the scale, scores at 6 weeks, 3 months and 12 months in the boot arm were compared with the Friedman test in patients with all three measurements, with Kendall's W as the effect size.
>
> **Results:** Among 50 of the 60 patients randomized to a boot, those with all three measurements, the median EFAS score was 12.5 (IQR 11 to 14) at 6 weeks, 17 (IQR 16 to 20) at 3 months and 20 (IQR 19 to 22) at 12 months (Friedman χ² = 84.9, df = 2, p < 0.001; Kendall's W = 0.85, one-sided 95% CI 0.78 to 1.00).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: the Friedman test ignores how big the changes are
It only uses each patient's ranking of the visits. A patient who gained 1 point and one who gained 10 count the same. Report the medians (or the changes) so readers can see the size of the improvement, and judge it against the MCID ([page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd#effect-sizes)).
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: data formats
R's `friedman.test()` takes a formula, `outcome ~ visit | patient`, on long data. pingouin's `friedman()` also takes long data; scipy's `friedmanchisquare()` instead wants one column per visit in wide data. All three correct for tied scores within a patient, so they agree.
:::

## Cochran's Q test {#cochran-q}

**The question:** Does walking-aid use change over the first year after surgery?

### When to use it

- A **yes/no** outcome measured **three or more times** on the same patients (or once on each member of a matched set).
- It extends [McNemar's test](07-two-paired-groups.qmd#mcnemar) to more than two visits, and, like McNemar's, it only learns from patients whose answer changed.
- Only patients measured at **every** visit are included.

### Look at the data first

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

aid <- proms |>
  select(case_id, visit, walking_aid) |>
  group_by(case_id) |>
  filter(all(!is.na(walking_aid))) |>    # keep patients measured at all four visits
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, levels = c("preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr")))

aid |>
  group_by(visit) |>
  summarise(patients = n(), using_aid = sum(walking_aid), percent = 100 * mean(walking_aid))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 4 × 4
  visit patients using_aid percent
  <fct>    <int>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 preop      328       114    34.8
2 6wk        328       194    59.1
3 3mo        328        80    24.4
4 1yr        328        34    10.4
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd
import pingouin as pg
from scipy import stats

proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")
visits = ["preop", "6wk", "3mo", "1yr"]

aid = proms[["case_id", "visit", "walking_aid"]]
complete = aid.groupby("case_id")["walking_aid"].transform(lambda answers: answers.notna().all())
aid = aid[complete]                     # keep patients measured at all four visits

print(aid.groupby("visit")["walking_aid"].agg(["count", "sum", "mean"]).loc[visits])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
       count    sum      mean
visit                        
preop    328  114.0  0.347561
6wk      328  194.0  0.591463
3mo      328   80.0  0.243902
1yr      328   34.0  0.103659
```


:::
:::

:::

328 patients answered at all four visits. A third used a walking aid before surgery, more than half at 6 weeks, and one in ten at 1 year.

### Run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
aid_test <- DescTools::CochranQTest(walking_aid ~ visit | case_id, data = aid)   # outcome ~ visit | patient
aid_test
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Cochran's Q test

data:  walking_aid and visit and case_id
Q = 186.79, df = 3, p-value < 2.2e-16
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
aid_test = pg.cochran(data=aid, dv="walking_aid", within="visit", subject="case_id")
print(aid_test)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
        Source  dof           Q         p_unc
cochran  visit    3  186.792711  3.008880e-40
```


:::
:::

:::





### Read the output

- **Q = 186.8, df = 3:** Cochran's Q statistic, with four visits minus one degrees of freedom.
- **p < 0.001** (R prints "p < 2.2e-16"): walking-aid use this different across visits would be very unlikely if it hadn't changed.

### Effect size and 95% CI

Cochran's Q has no standard single effect size. Describe the **proportion at each visit**, with its 95% CI (the Wilson interval from [page 4](04-describe-one-group.qmd#proportion)), and the changes between visits in percentage points.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
aid_by_visit <- aid |> group_by(visit) |> summarise(using = sum(walking_aid), patients = n())
aid_ci <- mapply(function(k, n) prop.test(k, n, correct = FALSE)$conf.int, aid_by_visit$using, aid_by_visit$patients)

aid_by_visit |>
  mutate(percent = 100 * using / patients, ci_low = 100 * aid_ci[1, ], ci_high = 100 * aid_ci[2, ])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 4 × 6
  visit using patients percent ci_low ci_high
  <fct> <dbl>    <int>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>
1 preop   114      328    34.8  29.8     40.1
2 6wk     194      328    59.1  53.8     64.3
3 3mo      80      328    24.4  20.1     29.3
4 1yr      34      328    10.4   7.51    14.1
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
counts = aid.groupby("visit")["walking_aid"].agg(["sum", "count"]).loc[visits]
cis = [stats.binomtest(int(k), int(n)).proportion_ci(method="wilson") for k, n in zip(counts["sum"], counts["count"])]

print(pd.DataFrame({"percent": 100 * counts["sum"] / counts["count"],
                    "ci_low": [100 * ci.low for ci in cis], "ci_high": [100 * ci.high for ci in cis]}))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
         percent     ci_low    ci_high
visit                                 
preop  34.756098  29.806008  40.059120
6wk    59.146341  53.750541  64.330383
3mo    24.390244  20.056804  29.316611

```


:::
:::

:::





Use rose by 24.4 percentage points from pre-op to 6 weeks, then fell well below its pre-op level by 1 year (24.4 points lower).

### How to report it

> **Methods:** Walking-aid use at the four visits was compared with Cochran's Q test in patients assessed at all four. Proportions are reported with Wilson 95% CIs.
>
> **Results:** Among 328 patients assessed at all four visits, walking-aid use was 34.8% (95% CI 29.8% to 40.1%) before surgery, 59.1% (95% CI 53.8% to 64.3%) at 6 weeks, 24.4% (95% CI 20.1% to 29.3%) at 3 months and 10.4% (95% CI 7.5% to 14.1%) at 1 year (Cochran's Q = 186.8, df = 3, p < 0.001).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: Q doesn't tell you the direction
Use went **up** and then **down**. Cochran's Q only says it wasn't the same at every visit. To say which changes are real, compare pairs of visits with McNemar's test and a correction for multiple comparisons ([page 15](../beyond/15-post-hoc.qmd#after-cochran-q)).
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: where to find Cochran's Q
Base R doesn't have Cochran's Q; `DescTools::CochranQTest()` (or `rstatix::cochran_qtest()`) does. In Python, pingouin's `cochran()` takes long data; statsmodels' `cochrans_q()` takes a wide array with one column per visit. All give the same Q.
:::

## Stratified Cox regression {#stratified-cox}

**The question:** In sets of three patients matched on procedure, age, sex, BMI and ASA class, does the risk of revision differ between implants A, B and C?

### When to use it

- The outcome is **time until an event**, and the patients come in **matched sets** of three or more.
- A Cox model **stratified** by matched set compares the implants only **within** sets, as on [page 7](07-two-paired-groups.qmd#stratified-cox), which used just the A and C patients from the same sets.
- With few events, expect wide CIs. [Page 14](../survival/14-cox-regression.qmd) covers Cox regression in full.

### Read the output

- **n = 156, number of events = 24:** 52 sets of three patients, 24 revisions.
- **exp(coef):** the hazard ratio of each implant against implant A, within matched sets. Implant B: 0.43; implant C: 3.91.
- **lower .95 / upper .95:** implant B's CI (0.08 to 2.25) is very wide and includes 1; implant C's (1.28 to 11.95) doesn't.
- **Likelihood ratio test = 13.5 on 2 df, p = 0.001:** the overall test that implant matters at all. Python prints it last.

### Effect size and 95% CI

The **hazard ratios** with their 95% CIs: within matched sets, implant C carried about four times the hazard of revision of implant A (3.91, 95% CI 1.28 to 11.95). The estimate for implant B (0.43, 95% CI 0.08 to 2.25) is too imprecise to interpret.

### How to report it

> **Methods:** Revision risk was compared between implants in matched sets using Cox regression stratified by set, with implant A as the reference.
>
> **Results:** In 52 sets of three patients matched on procedure, age, sex, BMI and ASA class, the hazard ratio for revision compared with implant A was 3.91 (95% CI 1.28 to 11.95) for implant C and 0.43 (95% CI 0.08 to 2.25) for implant B (likelihood ratio test for implant type, χ² = 13.5, df = 2, p = 0.001).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: only 24 events
A Cox model needs events, not just patients. With 24 revisions across three implants, the CIs are wide and the model can't support adjustment for anything else. [Page 14](../survival/14-cox-regression.qmd#choosing-covariates) covers how many events a model needs.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: strata and convergence
As on [page 7](07-two-paired-groups.qmd#stratified-cox), R puts `strata(set_id)` in the formula while lifelines takes `strata=["set_id"]`. Here lifelines' default convergence matches R exactly; with page 7's pairs it stopped a little early and needed `fit_options={"precision": 1e-9}`. If the two programs disagree in the fourth decimal, tighten it.
:::

## Which visits differ? {#which-groups-differ}

Each test above answers "is there any difference among the visits (or implants)?". When the answer is yes, the next question is which pairs differ. Comparing every pair with an ordinary paired test inflates the chance of a false positive: four visits make six pairs.

| After | Use | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Repeated-measures ANOVA | Paired t tests with Holm's adjustment | [15](../beyond/15-post-hoc.qmd#after-repeated-measures-anova) |
| Friedman | Pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank (or Conover) tests with Holm's adjustment | [15](../beyond/15-post-hoc.qmd#after-friedman) |
| Cochran's Q | Pairwise McNemar tests with Holm's adjustment | [15](../beyond/15-post-hoc.qmd#after-cochran-q) |
| Stratified Cox | Hazard ratios against a chosen reference | [14](../survival/14-cox-regression.qmd) |

For repeated PROMs, a [mixed model](../beyond/16-mixed-models.qmd#why-mixed-models) answers both questions at once (does the score change, and at which visits?) while keeping patients who missed a visit.
